outcome: A preprint by Simon Brendle and Pei-Ken Hung (arXiv:2608.19068, posted 19 August 2026) claims to construct a Riemannian metric of everywhere positive sectional curvature on S^2 x S^2, which would refute the product form of the Hopf conjecture (that no product of two positive-dimensional closed manifolds admits positive sectional curvature). The claim is very recent, has not been digested by the expert community or accepted by a journal, and an AI research-verification tool flagged apparently unresolved gaps (a bug in the supporting Mathematica calculation and a gap in a uniform bound) within a day of posting.

ai.basis_quote: This preprint is causing a stir in math because the title refutes the famous Hopf conjecture. This thread reports on some flaws that @RefineDotInk says need to be resolved for the argument to be sound. It's also a demo of what Refine (an AI research verifier) can do. ... The first apparent problem is that a key reduction supporting the 'second order positivity' needed uses a calculation that rests on a bug in the Mathematica code. The second major issue claims a gap in a uniform bound, where the AI believes this gap can be closed but isn't confident enough to complete the argument and asks the authors to do so.

counterexample.object: A metric of everywhere positive sectional curvature on S^2 x S^2, constructed as a third-order perturbation of a Cheeger-deformed ('Cheeger-Müter') metric on the standard product.
counterexample.verified_how: Claimed via an explicit analytic construction with symbolic-computation support in Mathematica (code attached to the arXiv submission); not yet independently verified by human experts, and an AI verifier (Refine) reported an apparent bug in the Mathematica calculation and an unresolved gap in a uniform bound shortly after posting.

disputes.summary: An AI research-verification system (Refine, from RefineDotInk) publicly reported, about a day after the preprint appeared, that a key calculation supporting 'second order positivity' rests on a bug in the authors' Mathematica code, and that there is a gap in a uniform bound the AI could not close itself. The authors issued a v2 on 24 August 2026 described only as correcting 'typographical errors in the manuscript and in the Mathematica notebook' — it is unclear from available sources whether this addresses the substantive issues Refine raised, or only cosmetic ones.

summary: The Wikipedia bullet covers 'the Hopf conjectures' (plural) on curvature and Euler characteristic of higher-dimensional Riemannian manifolds, which per the problem's own article and MathWorld comprises both a 'sign form' (positive sectional curvature on an even-dimensional closed manifold implies positive Euler characteristic) and a 'product form' (no product of two positive-dimensional closed manifolds admits everywhere positive sectional curvature — motivated by the fact that S^2 x S^2 has Euler characteristic 4 > 0, so the sign form alone would not rule it out). The sign form remains completely open in dimension >= 6 with no relevant results found in the window (only unrelated variant/case papers, e.g. Kennard-Mouillé-Nienhaus 2025 on positive second intermediate Ricci curvature with high-rank torus symmetry, and a curvature-operator-decomposition paper (arXiv:2507.15237) settling locally-conformally-flat and small-Weyl-curvature cases — both are restrictions/variants of the sign form, not resolutions of it). The one substantive, in-scope development is Brendle-Hung's August 2026 preprint (arXiv:2608.19068) claiming an explicit metric of positive sectional curvature on S^2 x S^2, which if correct refutes the product form outright (a genuine case of 'this problem', not a variant, since the product form is one of the two Hopf conjectures the bullet names) while leaving the sign form untouched. This is not yet resolved: there is no journal acceptance, no expert blog digestion (checked Terence Tao's blog, which has 2026 posts on other conjectures but none found on this one), and, notably, an AI verification tool (Refine) publicly identified apparently unresolved technical gaps (a bug underlying a key Mathematica-based calculation, and an unclosed gap in a uniform bound) within roughly a day of the preprint's posting. Only a minor v2 revision (typo fixes) has since appeared, so it is unclear the substantive issues were fixed. I classify status as 'claimed' (preprint with an unresolved correctness dispute, no expert digestion) rather than 'progress'/'incident', because the paper has not been withdrawn and the authors have not conceded the argument is broken — but I flag real uncertainty here. The AI role is coded 'incident' rather than 'assisted' or 'none': Refine is an AI system that produced a substantive technical finding (an identified bug and an identified gap) about the mathematical content of a claimed resolution, and that claim's correctness is now publicly disputed as a direct consequence of AI-driven checking — this is the pattern of an AI-associated claim/dispute, not merely AI-as-tool assistance to the authors (the authors' own Mathematica usage is computer algebra, not an AI system, and is not disclosed as AI-generated mathematics). I use 'incident' with reservations since the underlying human claim has not been withdrawn, only publicly disputed on correctness grounds by an AI verifier; see competing_reading.
competing_reading: Two alternative readings are plausible. (1) Status: if the v2 revision (24 August 2026) in fact silently fixed the substantive gaps Refine flagged (not just typos, despite the changelog wording), the correct status could be 'claimed' moving toward 'resolved' pending expert digestion, with the Refine episode better treated as `progress`/an anecdote in summary rather than driving `ai_role`. Conversely, if the Refine-identified bug is fatal and unfixed, this may eventually resolve to `progress`/`incident` with `resolution_direction` null (the counterexample claim withdrawn), which would also change ai_role interpretation. (2) ai_role: one could argue for 'none' on grounds that Refine did not produce mathematics that appears 'in' any accepted result — it only critiqued an unverified claim, and the underlying construction is entirely human-and-Mathematica. I retained 'incident' because the guidance defines that code as 'an AI-produced claim that was announced or machine-verified, then withdrawn' or, by extension, publicly disputed via AI-driven verification with the claim's status left unresolved; but a stricter reading limiting 'incident' to claims of AI-generated proofs (as opposed to AI-generated critiques of human proofs) would push this toward 'none' with the Refine episode reported only as a dispute/summary note, not a role code.
what_would_settle_it: Whether Brendle-Hung's construction is ultimately confirmed correct (via expert digestion, journal acceptance, or a further arXiv revision that explicitly addresses and resolves the Refine-flagged bug and uniform-bound gap) or withdrawn/found fatally flawed; and separately, an authoritative account (from the authors, from Refine/RefineDotInk, or from expert commentary) of whether the AI-identified issues were real, and whether v2's changes addressed them.

corrections.why: Reviewed and retained, with the reservation the researching agent already recorded. The code does not fit its own definition (`incident` = an AI-produced claim later withdrawn): the claim is human (Brendle-Hung, with Mathematica, which is computer algebra and not an AI system), the AI arrived afterwards from outside as a critic, and nothing has been withdrawn. `none` is defensible on DEEP_DIVE.md 6.2, which excludes checking. The consequence is handled downstream instead: `incident` is excluded from AI-involved counts, so this row does not enter any AI numerator. Note that it is also a counterexample row, so the exclusion moves it into the non-AI column of the counterexample split; applying the same rules to `bound` (see moving-sofa-problem), that split becomes 11/25 = 44% AI-credited against 8/34 = 24% without, rather than 12/27 = 44% against 7/32 = 22%.

corrections.by: hand correction by a human reviewer, not the researching agent and not any automated pass
corrections.supersedes: the 2026-09-24 ai_role entry above, which retained `incident` with reservations
corrections.why: Overturning that retention. `incident` is defined in §6.1 and §6.2 as an AI-PRODUCED claim that was announced or machine-verified and then withdrawn, and neither half of that describes this row. The claim is human: Brendle and Hung constructed a metric of everywhere positive sectional curvature on S^2 x S^2, with Mathematica, which is computer algebra and not an AI system. Refine arrived from outside about a day later and ATTACKED the claim, reporting a bug under a key second-order-positivity calculation and an unclosed gap in a uniform bound. And nothing has been withdrawn: the preprint stands, the authors have not conceded, and the v2 of 24 August 2026 is described as typographical. An AI arguing that a human claim is WRONG is not AI involvement in producing it. §6.2 is explicit that using a model to check work is `none`, however substantive the check, and the researching agent's own `competing_reading` proposed `none` on exactly these grounds. STATUS IS UNCHANGED at `claimed`: a claim publicly disputed on correctness grounds is still a claim, and an AI attacking it does not make the row any different from any other contested claim. The Refine episode is not erased — it stays in `summary`, `disputes` and `ai.basis_quote` as evidence of what happened, and it is one of the more interesting things in this dataset; it simply stops being counted as an AI contribution to the Hopf conjecture. EFFECT ON THE NUMBERS: AI-involved resolutions fall from 27 of 59 to 26; because this row rests on an exhibited counterexample, it also moves a counterexample from the AI column to the human one, so the split in AUDIT.md §6 becomes 11 of 26 AI-involved (42%) against 8 of 33 without (24%), rather than 12 of 27 (44%) against 7 of 32 (22%). The direction of that finding is unchanged; the gap narrows from 2.0x to 1.75x. NOTE THE DEPARTURE: §6.1 and §6.2 as written offer no code for an AI that refereed someone else's mathematics, so this row is filed under `none` for want of anywhere better. That is a gap in the coding scheme, not a judgement that Refine did nothing.

judgement.doubts: Agree with the current codes. The bullet names the Hopf conjectures in the plural (F2), so refuting the product form alone is a case, and the row is partial whatever verification the claim eventually gets. Refine only criticised the work, so ai_role is none (F9); the Refine quote in ai.basis_quote is about that criticism, not any AI contribution. The 2507.* papers are coded variant because the record calls them restrictions or variants; if the second one really settles a class of manifolds under the sign form's own hypotheses it would be a case, but it would not beat this row. Correctness is unresolved: the Refine findings come from unread snippets, and nobody has checked whether v2 fixes them. If the authors withdraw or concede, the row falls to open.
